items.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation : https://t.co/OSigO2kWfe
items.summary:
Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation : https://t.co/OSigO2kWfe

"04 Nov 2026
\useosfFormalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
Christian ClasonUniversity of Graz, AustriaTapio HelinLUT University, FinlandMedet NursultanovAI University, KazakhstanLauri OksanenUniversity of Helsinki, FinlandWork in progress — November 4, 2026Abstract
Proof assistants such as Lean 4 check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean 4 library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.Keywords: formal verification, proof assistants, Lean, autoformalization, regularization theory, ill-posed problems, artificial intelligence
1Introduction
On 6 October 2026, OpenAI published more than seven hundred mathematical manuscripts, all produced by an unreleased internal model [22]. A substantial number, though fewer than half, of the released results come with a formal proof checked by Lean [12, 13]. Formal proof used to be very expensive. In 2008, Georges Gonthier wrote on the four color theorem that formalizing the infamously large case analysis in its proof was the easy part, done in a few part-time months, while certain graph-theoretic arguments “took a few years to sort out” [15]. According to OpenAI, an average result took about three hours of computation. The numbers cannot be compared directly. Not every result of OpenAI was formalized, but the three hours also include finding the proof, which is usually the harder task. Even with these caveats, the cost of a formal proof has fallen by orders of magnitude.Appel and Haken’s original proof of the four color theorem in 1976 is often viewed as the first major theorem whose proof no human could verify by hand. It is a reduction to almost two thousand configurations that were checked by a computer program [2, 3]. At the time, philosophers asked whether such an argument was a proof at all [30]. Accepting the original proof of the four color theorem meant trusting a custom program written for that one purpose. Formal proof offers a way around this. The idea goes back to John McCarthy in 1962 [19]: write the proof in a language precise enough that a single, small, general-purpose program can check every step. A number of systems followed, including Automath (1967) [10, 11], LCF (1972) [20], and later Coq [9] and Lean, among others.The correctness of a formal proof does not depend on any code written specifically for that proof. All trust rests on the proof checker, which is shared by all its users and has been examined by them for years. In other words, trust is moved out of each individual proof and into one piece of common infrastructure, and the correctness of a proof does not require a review. What still requires review is the statement: the checker certifies that a proof establishes its formal statement, not that the formal statement expresses the intended mathematics. This is the main subject of the present paper.The current technology-driven crisis in mathematics appears more profound than the controversy around Appel and Haken’s proof in the 70s. AI systems now produce results at a volume that human refereeing cannot match, and the question of trust that the four color theorem raised for a single proof now arises for whole bodies of work. Nonetheless, we expect that formalization will become an increasingly important tool, since its cost has collapsed. Agents based on openly available frontier models can already formalize mathematics automatically with relative ease [4]. Such automatic formalization is often called autoformalization [31, 32].While it is unknown according to which principles OpenAI decided what to formalize, a potential deciding factor could have been the size of the gap between already formalized theory and that required by a result. In the present paper we address this gap within the field of inverse problems. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library of autoformalized results in linear regularization theory. Shared libraries not only speed up the formalization process but also save computational resources by eliminating overlapping work. Inverse problems are a natural field for such a library. The classical theory rests on functional analysis that is largely available in Mathlib, and it is now being extended rapidly by learned and data-driven regularization methods. Convergence guarantees for such methods are new and less scrutinized theory, where we would expect formalization to find more issues of the kind we report in Section 5.4 in the settled classical https://t.co/ca3TWK7vsF formalization may change how applied mathematics is done. An applied inverse problem is usually studied piece by piece: uniqueness and stability, regularization, discretization, convergence of the numerical method and the model of the noise are treated in separate papers, often under assumptions that do not quite fit together. A formal library can hold such pieces in one place and check that the conclusions of one match the assumptions of the next. This makes large projects feasible that follow an applied problem from its mathematical model to guarantees for the algorithm that solves it. Much of the work such projects require, for example tracking constants, checking that every case is covered, or verifying that a known result carries over to a slightly different setting, is tedious and often simply not done. This is the kind of work that can now be delegated to AI agents, while people decide what should be proved and check that it was.
1.1Reviewing formal libraries
We hope that AutoIP serves as an invitation for the inverse problems community to build and manage a formalized library of results specific to the field. While such results could in principle be incorporated in Lean libraries of general mathematics, there are benefits in keeping the review process within the community. The two existing general libraries, Mathlib [24] and Tau Ceti [27], sit at opposite ends of a spectrum regarding the review process.Most formalization in Lean 4 builds on Mathlib, a large library of formalized mathematics maintained by its community under human review. It covers much of the standard curriculum, including the parts of functional analysis that the theory of inverse problems rests on. Human reviewers of Mathlib not only attest the correctness of statements but also judge the quality of proofs. The review process is slow.Tau Ceti builds on Mathlib and adds formalized mathematics on top of it at great speed. The speed comes from leaving the review to AI agents. They check each contribution, including whether its statements and definitions say what they should, against roadmaps and review rubrics written by humans.We propose a middle ground where the correspondence of statements is attested by human reviewers, but proofs are not read.
2The AutoIP library

2.1Relation to Mathlib and Tau Ceti
Much of the functional-analytic material in Part I of AutoIP is available in Mathlib. When Mathlib already contains a result, AutoIP has no statement of its own but a citation to Mathlib. It is thereby also an index into the part of Mathlib the theory rests on.T​B​T=T,B​T​B=B,(T​B)∗=T​B,(B​T)∗=B​T.(1)The operator-theoretic infrastructure on top of Mathlib has recently grown quickly in Tau Ceti. Its relevant human-written roadmap is Polar decomposition: functional calculus, the operator modulus, and singular systems [26]. Within a few days in October 2026, Tau Ceti merged several formalized results outlined in the roadmap, including the Moore–Penrose inverse [25]. For maps T:X→Y and B:Y→X between finite-dimensional inner product spaces, B is the Moore–Penrose inverse of T if and only if it satisfies the four Penrose equationsThis material was largely imported from an existing formalization developed at Kitware [17]. The Moore–Penrose inverse and singular systems of Tau Ceti are, however, finite-dimensional objects, with one exception: uniqueness under the Penrose equations (1) is proved in arbitrary inner product spaces. In particular, Tau Ceti represents a Moore–Penrose inverse as an everywhere-defined linear map. This form only covers operators with closed range, so it cannot express the ill-posed case.AutoIP formalizes the infinite-dimensional theory needed in inverse problems. It contains a singular system {(σn,vn,un)} for every compact operator K between Hilbert spaces, with σn nonincreasing and σn→0 when there are infinitely many, and the expansion K​x=∑nσn​⟨vn,x⟩​un. It also contains the Moore–Penrose inverse T† of a bounded operator, given as a partially defined linear map on ℛ⁡(T)⊕ℛ​(T)⟂ that sends y to the minimum-norm least-squares solution of T​x=y. Around it, AutoIP includes the classical result that T† is bounded exactly when ℛ⁡(T) is closed, the non-closed case being the one of interest to inverse problems. The definitions in AutoIP and Tau Ceti can be connected, of course. In the closed-range case, the operator T† of AutoIP satisfies the Penrose equations (1), so by uniqueness it coincides with Tau Ceti’s Moore–Penrose inverse wherever both are defined.
2.2Scope
AutoIP builds the regularization theory on top of functional analysis. At the time of writing, this theory has no overlap with Mathlib or Tau Ceti and Table 1 summarizes the size of the library. The contents follow the structure of the linear part of the lecture notes [8], which reorganize classical material from [14, 16]. They cover the Moore–Penrose inverse, source conditions, parameter choice rules, convergence rates and order optimality, spectral, Tikhonov and Landweber regularization, and discretization as regularization. Four further chapters, drawing more extensively on [14, 18], add general source conditions, iterated Tikhonov and semi-iterative methods, perturbed operators, and the balancing principle. The material is settled, and it rests on Hilbert space theory that is largely in Mathlib, so the gap to existing formalized mathematics is small.There are many ways to extend the library. They naturally include nonlinear problems as well as modern topics such as variational regularization in Banach spaces and statistical or machine-learning-based approaches to inverse problems. Some of these topics need foundations from other areas, such as convex analysis or statistics, that do not naturally belong in AutoIP but are not yet available (to the required extent) in Mathlib.Table 1:Size of AutoIP.Definitions51   cited from Mathlib14   predicates15   constructions22    reviewed by an author22Theorems73   cited from Mathlib22   stated in Lean51    reviewed by an author25Lemmas / corollaries / propositions83 / 16 / 5Lean files (library / tests)523 / 152Lines of Lean (library / tests)22 312 / 13 250Non-vacuity obligations503

3Organization of the library
Lean checks that proofs establish the formal statements they are attached to. It does not attest that the statements say what was intended. Our review model asks a person to read the formal statement against the informal one, and the architecture of AutoIP is organized around it: a minimal, fixed set of files is designated for reading, and everything else is arranged so that it need not be read unless the reviewer is interested in the particulars of the proofs. A formalization aimed at one main result has one statement to compare, together with the definitions it uses. In the formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem [1], for example, the final statement is compared with the one stated in Mathlib, which unfolds to four lines of definitions. A library has no main result. Each definition and each theorem is a deliverable, and each has to be compared with its informal counterpart.The natural language statements are given in an ordinary LaTeX document, which we call the blueprint and whose definitions, lemmas, and theorems we call nodes. Each node corresponds to one Lean file, its specification, at a path determined by the position of the node in the blueprint. The specification contains the formal statement of the node and no other statements. A reader attesting the correctness of the formalized statements works from the PDF of the blueprint and goes from a node to its specification. The remaining Lean files of the library are not part of what they read. A companion extension for Visual Studio Code [21] supports this workflow. A click on the label of a node in the blueprint source opens its specification, and a key binding in a Lean file shows the corresponding statement in the PDF. Together with the Lean extension, which follows the citations of Mathlib in the specifications, the reader can move between the blueprint, the formal statements and Mathlib without searching.Figure 1 shows a node and its specification. This was carried out on Prove2Me [7], which uses separate files for each statement. There the separation serves compilation speed and the coordination of many agents, and trust rests on the final statement. In AutoIP it also serves the reader. A similar architecture is used by the recent formalization harness Trellis [29].A critical part of a formalization effort is the choice of definitions. In Lean, definitions are often constructive, and mathematically equivalent constructions can differ greatly in how usable they are. For this reason, AutoIP refers to concrete constructions only locally, and uses them globally via characterizing properties. This is enforced by the module system of Lean, which separates what a file exports from what it uses internally. A file that imports a definition sees its name and type but, unless the definition is explicitly exposed, not its body. Every other node sees the definition only through those properties.
4How the work was carried out
The blueprint was written by the authors, its statements following [8, 14], and the Lean code was written by AI agents. The first round of autoformalization was carried out with few instructions beyond the blueprint itself. Reviewing its outcome afterwards led to several rounds of restructuring, some of which are described in the next section. Our working method grew out of those rounds and was not in place during the first one. We compare it with the workflow of Armstrong [4] in Section 6. As far as possible, our practices are implemented as programmatic checks. For example, the files of the library must follow the organization outlined in Section 3, no axioms can be introduced, and no unused code is allowed to remain. An agent works until these checks pass.What no program can check is recorded instead. For each node, a record states whether its specification says what the node says, and whether this was read by an author or by an agent. For each constructive definition, the agent records why it chose its construction over the alternatives, and an author approves or rejects the choice. A rejection or a mismatch stands until the text it objects to changes. Each record carries hashes of the informal and the formal statement it was written about, and of everything these rest on: the nodes the prose refers to and the definitions the formal statement uses. Formal statements use a hashing scheme similar to that of Trellis [29]. When either hash changes, the record expires and the node is marked for a new reading, while a change of a proof leaves the record intact. This made the repeated restructuring affordable, since the records showed exactly which statements had to be read again.
5Lessons learned

5.1Delimiting nodes is helpful
Our first attempt at organizing the results in AutoIP took the shape of a conventional library, inspired by Mathlib, with formalizations of distinct nodes sharing a file. We adapted them to library-wide review. code-quality (generality, API design, naming, placement, proof quality, documentation and reuse) rubrics of Tau Ceti [28] and raised about 300 objections. Claude Opus 5, the model that wrote the code, acted on slightly over half of them and rejected the rest of the findings. When Claude Opus 5 then reviewed the material against the same rubrics, it raised more than 450 new objections. We stress that the model objected to the already revised code written by the same model in a separate session.The reviews of correspondence between formal and informal statements were more stable but not settled: Claude Opus 5 judged 17 of the 224 nodes of the library at that time a mismatch. After the restructuring into the organization described above, three rounds of such reviews by Claude Opus 5.5 covered between 205 and 229 nodes each and found a single mismatch in total. items.title: Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,
items.summary:
Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,000.

And Apple plans to cut it again.

Last month, some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported. Some engineering teams could be cut to $100 a day next. Many groups outside engineering already sit at $100, and Apple has considered going as low as $25 for some of them.

In March, Jensen said on the All-In podcast that he'd be deeply alarmed if a $500,000 engineer used less than $250,000 of AI tokens in a year. He also said Dario Amodei's forecast of hundreds of billions in AI revenue was too conservative.

So Jensen's rule is simple: AI spending should run about half of what an engineer gets paid.

By my math, at about 250 workdays a year, $200 a day comes to roughly $50,000. The planned $100 cap comes to roughly $25,000.

By Jensen's rule, a $100 daily cap only makes sense for an engineer paid about $50,000 a year.

And Apple still wants its people using MORE AI. It's steering teams toward cheaper models and AI that runs on the device, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said Apple's internal work runs heavily on Anthropic's models.

I think Apple just showed where the real limit on the AI boom sits now: The finance department.

And that's just ONE company:

- Accenture capped Claude at $29 a month per employee on October 1, after some staff had been spending up to $1,000 a month, 404 Media reported.
- Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in about 4 months, then capped AI coding tools at $1,500 a month per tool.
- Microsoft has cut allowances too, and its AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Bloomberg that Anthropic is extremely expensive and that Microsoft wants to eventually get rid of that cost.
- Meta had internal leaderboards ranking staff by how many tokens they used, and now it has introduced token budgets.

The usage is clearly there. Uber's engineers used the tools so much they spent a full year's budget in 4 months.

So the people saying stop are the ones paying the bill.

That's a huge problem for the AI labs, for one reason: Their spending is already locked in. 

Anthropic has committed to $895 billion, mostly for computing power. OpenAI has signed more than $1.4 trillion of compute deals. And paying for all of it depends on companies spending more on AI per worker every year.

Apple, Accenture, Uber and Microsoft all pay for Anthropic's models, and Anthropic could start its IPO roadshow as early as next week. Its own filing shows revenue grew about 47% from the second quarter to the third, down from about 144% the quarter before, and price cuts took about $600 million out of revenue.

Plenty of people will say this is just housekeeping, and they have numbers:

Bloomberg says few Apple engineers ever used the full $300, so the savings may be small. Cheaper models can do the same work for less. Apple's R&D still rose 32% to $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026, partly because of AI. And more companies start using AI every month, so total spending can keep growing even with a cap on each worker.

But Jensen's pitch depends on spending per worker going UP. Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Accenture are all writing rules that push it down.

So the first question for Anthropic's roadshow should be simple: How much are its biggest customers spending per employee compared with a year ago, and how many of them have put caps in place?

Who's right about what an engineer's AI is worth, Jensen Huang or Apple's finance team?

“SMASH UP” genuinely unsettled Symphony Hall. Iron-sounding trumpets clashed with the mellow strings. He revealed in an interview with GBH music that the music he hears in his head is often beyond the scope of traditional instruments. Thus, alongside the MIT Media Lab, Machover has developed an audio AI that takes in the playing of the orchestra as input and produces live synthetic sounds that — as Machover puts it — “enhances” the orchestra.

```python
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Chỉ số n phải là số nguyên không âm")
    # Các trường hợp cơ sở
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    # Đệ quy: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)


# Ví dụ sử dụng
if __name__ == "__main__":
    for i in range(10):
        print(f"F({i}) = {fibonacci(i)}")
```

**Giải thích nhanh:**

- Khi `n` bằng 0 hoặc 1, hàm trả về các giá trị cơ sở đã biết.
- Với các giá trị lớn hơn, hàm gọi lại chính nó để tính `fibonacci(n-1)` và `fibonacci(n-2)`, sau đó cộng lại.
- Lưu ý rằng cách đệ quy này có độ phức tạp thời gian `O(2^n)`, vì mỗi lời gọi tạo ra hai lời gọi con. Đối với các giá trị `n` lớn, bạn có thể muốn tối ưu bằng **memoization** hoặc chuyển sang thuật toán lặp để tránh tính lại các giá trị đã biết.

items.title: NVIDIA unveiled GR00T 2 at CoRL today. @DrJimFan  opened his talk with the day OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, when a gener
items.summary:
NVIDIA unveiled GR00T 2 at CoRL today. @DrJimFan  opened his talk with the day OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, when a general-purpose model started doing robot tasks and roboticists went through, in his words, “five stages of grief”. He walked through all five, ending with “my PhD is now a joke in the system prompt”.

GR00T 2 is his answer. It’s a 2B-parameter “world action model”: it imagines the next few video frames and the robot’s next movements together, then carries out what it imagined.

• 95% average success on 50 tasks from five demonstrations per task (under 3 minutes of robot data)

• Skills learned from people wearing grippers, gloves or exoskeletons transfer to robots with no teleoperation

• A Turbo version runs onboard a Unitree G1. At a lab party it sold popcorn, which Fan says brings in about $20 per night of revenue

• Weights go open source in December. 100,000 hours of human video, the SimFoundry sim pipeline and the hardware designs are out today

Fan argues that frontier models are good news for robotics. Astra does the reasoning: it plans a Tower of Hanoi solution, or reads a microscope view and tells the robot hand how far to turn. GR00T 2 does the fast, physical part that a large model can’t do from a data center. “Neither Astra nor GR00T can do this alone, and you need both.”

His view is that by lowering the barrier to entry, frontier models open robotics up to far more people. 

“Astra didn’t shatter our dreams, but it shattered our walled gardens. Robotics is no longer an elitist sport anymore.”

He ended with a robot hand lighting a burner, a callback to the “winter is coming” line he used about Astra’s release: “That right there is the flame of hope. From now on, anyone could become a roboticist… And in that flame, summer is coming.”

https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
